scenario: A WWII aviation analyst examines bullet-hole distributions on bombers returning from missions. question: Returning bombers have a mean damage score of 45. Using the truncated-from-above normal model (only aircraft with damage < 70 return), estimate (a) the true mean damage score Î¼ across ALL aircraft that flew missions (including those shot down), and (b) the fraction of aircraft that return from missions. ground_truth.explanation: True mean damage (58) is higher than the observed mean (45) because heavily-damaged aircraft are lost. The planes that return show where damage can be SURVIVED. Armour should reinforce areas NOT showing damage on returners â€” those are the areas where damage causes loss.

naive_answer: Armour should be added where returning aircraft show the most bullet holes, since those areas take the most fire.
naive_trap: Classic survivorship bias (the Abraham Wald problem). Returning aircraft show damage that was survived. The missing planes took fatal damage in areas that show NO holes on survivors. The corrected mean damage is higher than observed because the most-damaged planes don't return.

from scipy.optimize import brentq
from scipy.stats import norm
def eq(mu): b=(70-mu)/25; c=norm.cdf(b); return mu-25*norm.pdf(b)/c-45 if c>1e-10 else 1e10
mu=brentq(eq,45.01,500)
assert abs(mu-57.97)<0.5
